I have a bunch of 'refactoring' which I think would be great to do. I'm curious if anyone knows the capability of AI in this area, and how best to be used.

In particular, I am curious to see if anyone can get an AI model to do the refactoring described in this GitHub issue:

  • Physlib#1042

I know roughly what the PR should look like for this issue, and I'm curious to know how much the AI output aligns with my expectations.

I've been experimenting with Claude Code. As you know, I'm trying to build a library for thermodynamics. With @Jay Yarlott and another student we've proved a few things from the ground up and I've attempted to synthesize a refactoring that can provide strong foundations and downstream usability. I have definitely made progress and I think we have a good design now (we'll present it to the community asap). Here are some general comments due to what I have experienced:

  • The AI helps me "exploring possible alternatives" in a faster way. Rather than imagining what happens if I define things in one way or another, I ask the AI to sketch the same proof in two ways and we brainstorm about why one is better and in what way
  • It will definitely lead you astray if you don't force it to take into account elements like re-usability of the code. I think this is the same issue with people on Mathlib complaining that AI-generated code might actually solve a theorem but the code it produces is not helpful to prove other stuff.
  • So, my conclusion (at least for now), is that I have to actively use it to brainstorm around what's the best way to do refactoring. Namely, I have to tell the AI the principles and ways in which I think a refactoring should be done. Once you do that (especially since you have more Lean knowledge than what me) in "Plan Mode", Claude will come up with a draft plan of how the refactoring looks like. Check the plan, iterate a few times to fix things, and then let it run on a test branch. This second part, where it writes the code after you agreed on the general plan, I find almost no issues. If I find an issue with that, I can typically trace that issue to some form of mistake I made in the conversation and in specifying what I needed. Sometimes it's due to my own ignorance about Lean, sometimes it's about design principles, rarely it's about bugs or code that does not work.

I hope this helps!
Many thanks @Fabio Anzà. In terms of practicalities, how do you actually do this (i.e. what software)? i'm assuming that lean-lsp-mcp is involved somewhere along the lines?
I use the Claude Code extension in VS Code so that I have three columns, side by side starting from the left: the file I'm working on, the Lean InfoView, Claude Code. See the image

Doing a bit of an experiment here: Physlib#1047 with another refactoring I've been meaning to do for a while. Ended up using GitHub copilot, because (I think) it makes everything public and connected to the PR, which I think is a desirable feature. The back-and-forth is pretty slow though, and haven't worked out how to effectively work on plan mode.
(Maybe one idea is to do the back-and-forth in the GitHub issue, or there is a way to get it to output its plan there.)

How do you mean

because (I think) it makes everything public and connected to the PR, which I think is a desirable feature.

In the sense that:

  1. The initial prompt is just this GitHub issue Physlib#1046. In theory anyone could comment on this, and add suggestions, and the AI model would use that information to make it's PR.
  2. The back-and-forth is done at Physlib#1047 with the normal 'review' comments that someone would put on human PRs. Again, in theory, anyone could provide a review to that PR and those would be taken into account by the AI in the next iteration.

I think this is desirable, because it means that everything is 'openly developed'. However, as I understand it, these GitHub copilot workflows are not the best which are out there. I'm guessing that Claude Code does do better response here.
